Tosafot on Bava Batra 30a:6:1.hebrew: לאו קמודית דהא ארעא דידי הוא - פי' רבינו שמואל: דאם מוחזק זה שלש שנים, וטוען "מפלניא זבנתיה דזבנה מינך קמי דידי" — דנאמן, במיגו דאי בעי אמר "מינך זבנתיה ואכלתיה שני חזקה". אי נמי אם יש לו עדים שהחזיק בה המוכר יום אחד — והביא ראיה מההיא דדר בקשתא בעיליתא דלקמן. וכדבריו כן הוא היכא דיש עדים למערער שהקרקע שלו היתה; אבל בעובדא דהכא משמע שלא היה למערער עדים, מדקאמר "לאו קא מודית כו'". אי הוה טעין "קמי דידי זבנה מינך" או "דר בה חד יומא" היה נאמן, אף על פי שלא החזיק שלש שנים, מיגו דאי בעי אמר "לא היתה שלך מעולם". אבל ודאי השתא דאמר "מפלניא זבינתה דזבנה מינך", והודה שהיתה שלו, תו לא מצי למיטען "קמי דידי זבנה מינך", או "קמי דידי דר בה חד יומא", מיגו דאי בעי אמר בתחלה "לא היתה שלך מעולם"; דמיגו למפרע לא אמרינן, כדמוכח לקמן (בבא בתרא דף מא:) גבי ההוא דדר בקשתא בעיליתא ארבע שנין, ואמר "מפלניא זבינתיה דזבנה מינך", אתא לקמיה דר' חייא, אמר ליה: "אייתי סהדי דדר ביה אפילו חד יומא, ואוקמי' לה בידך". משמע דאי לית ליה סהדי אין נאמן לומר "קמי דידי דר בה חד יומא", במיגו דאי בעי אמר "מינך זבינתיה"; כיון שכבר הודה דלאו מיניה זבנה, לית ליה תו מיגו, ואין לו להאמינו במאי דקאמר השתא, מתוך שהיה יכול לשקר בתחילה קודם שהודה — דלא הוה מסיק אדעתיה שהיה זקוק לטענה זו. והא דקאמר התם רב "וחזיתיה לדעתיה דחביבי, דאי הוה א"ל קמי דידי זבנה מינך הוה מהימן ליה, במיגו דאי בעי אמר מינך זבינתה" — לא קאמר שהיה עדיין נאמן בטענה זו, אלא כלומר: אי הוה טעין מעיקרא, קודם שהודה. וה"ה דאי הוה טעין מעיקרא "קמי דידי דר בה חד יומא" דהוה מהימן. ועוד ראיה מסוף דזה בורר (סנהדרין דף לא.) גבי ההיא איתתא דנפק שטרא מתותי ידה, אמרה "ידענא ליה בהאי שטרא דפריע הוא כו'", ולא הימנה רב נחמן. א"ל רבא: "והא אי בעיא קלתיה"; כיון דאתחזק בבי דינא, "אי בעיא קלתיה" לא אמרי'. אלמא אע"ג דקודם שראינוהו בידה היתה נאמנת לומר דפרוע הוא, במיגו דאי בעיא קלתי', השתא דאתחזק בבי דינא — פי' שראינוהו בידה — לא מהימנה, דאין כאן עוד מיגו, שעל כרחך צריכה עכשיו טענה זו שהיא אומרת, אם רוצה לפטור את הלוה. ובקונט' פי' שם: אתחזק — שהיה השטר מקוים. ואין נראה לר"י, דמה מועיל? דמ"מ אי בעיא קלתיה. ועוד ראיה, דתנן בפ' שבועת הדיינין (שבועות דף לח:): "מנה לי בידך", אמר לו "הן"; למחר א"ל "תנהו לי", "נתתיו לך" — פטור. ופריך מינה (שם מא.): למ"ד המלוה את חבירו בעדים צריך לפורעו בעדים, והא הכא כיון דתבעיה בעדים כמאן דאוזפיה בעדים דמי, וקתני פטור! ומאי קושיא? שאני הכא דפטור, מיגו דאי בעי אמר "אתמול לא היו דברים מעולם". אלא ודאי כי האי גוונא לא אמרינן מיגו. ומה שפ"ה בפ' בתרא דכתובות (דף קט: ושם) גבי עשאה סימן לאחר, דאם טען ואמר "חזרתי ולקחתיה ממנו לאחר שעשיתיה סימן בשמו" נאמן, דהפה שאסר הוא הפה שהתיר; דמאחר שיש עדים שהיתה שלו ונגזלה ממנו, אין לו זכות אלא על פיו של זה שעשאה סימן לו, והרי חזר ואמר "לקחתיה ממך" — אין נראה לר"י דבכי האי גוונא לא אמרי' מיגו, כדפרישית, דע"י מה שהיה יכול לטעון תחילה אינו נאמן עכשיו. אלא נראה לר"י דהתם נמי חזר ואכלה שני חזקה אחר שעשאה סימן. וכי תימא: אי אכלה שני חזקה — פשיטא! ומאי קמ"ל ר' יוחנן דנאמן? מתני' היא: "חזקה שיש עמה טענה הרי זו חזקה"! וי"ל דס"ד דלא מהימן, כיון שערער עליו קודם שאכלה שני חזקה לומר שהיא שלו, לא עביד איניש דליזבנה בתר הכי; קמ"ל. וכן ההוא עובדא דמייתי בתר הכי, איירי בשאכלה שני חזקה. ובעובדא דידן אי הוה מייתי המחזיק סהדי דדר ביה חד יומא, נראה לרשב"א דהוה לאוקומי לארעא בידיה, אע"ג דליכא מיגו; מ"מ טענינן ללוקח, מאחר שהיה המוכר נאמן לומר "זבינתה מינך", במיגו דאי בעי אמר "לא היתה שלך מעולם". ואף על גב דהאי לוקח ידע שהיתה שלו, והוי כחד סהדא, מכל מקום הוי מיגו, כדמשמע לקמן (בבא בתרא דף לג:) גבי נסכא דר' אבא: אי לא הוי מחויב שבועה ואינו יכול לישבע, היה נאמן לומר "דידי חטפי", במיגו דאי בעי אמר "לא חטפי", והיה מכחיש את העד; והכא לא הוי מחויב שבועה, דאין נשבעין על הקרקעות. וכה"ג מצינו בסוף המוכר (לקמן בבא בתרא דף ע.) גבי מפקיד אצל חבירו בשטר, דאע"ג דלא טענינן ליתמי "נאנסו", אפ"ה טענינן ליה "החזרתיו לך", כיון שאביהם היה נאמן בטענה זו, במיגו דאי בעי אמר "נאנסו". ואור"י דלא דמי לההיא דהמוכר את הבית; דהכא אם היה רוצה המוכר לזכות בטענה זו דלא היתה שלך מעולם, לא היה מעכבה הלוקח, שהרי יודע היה שהיתה שלו. כתב ר"ח: ראינו לרבותינו הגאונים ז"ל דהאי מחזיק לית ליה למיחת לדינא בהדי מריה דארעא, אלא האי דזבין ליה מחית בהדיה. ואין נראה לרשב"א, דהא כל זכות שתבא לידו מכר ראשון לשני, ולא יוכל לדחות ולומר לו "לאו בעל דברים דידי את". ולקמן אשכחן בהדיא גבי ההוא דדר בקשתא בעיליתא, דלא מצי למימר ליה "לאו בעל דברים דידי את"; אלא אי הוה משכח סהדי דדר ביה ההוא גברא חד יומא, הוה מוקי לה ר' חייא בידיה:
Tosafot on Bava Batra 30a:6:1.english: "Do you not admit that this land is mine?" - Rabbeinu Shmuel explained: If this one has been in possession for three years, and claims, "I bought it from so-and-so, who bought it from you in my presence" — he is believed, by virtue of a *migo*: for had he wished, he could have said, "I bought it from you and ate its produce for the years of *chazakah*." Alternatively, [the same applies] if he has witnesses that the seller possessed it for one day — and he brought proof from that case of the one who lived in the upper chamber in Kashta, [which appears] later. And according to his words, this is so where the claimant has witnesses that the land was his. But in the case here, it implies that the claimant had no witnesses, since [Rava] said, "Do you not admit, etc." If [the possessor] had claimed, "He bought it from you in my presence," or "He lived in it for one day," he would be believed, even though he did not possess it for three years, by virtue of a *migo*: for had he wished, he could have said, "It was never yours." But certainly now that he said, "I bought it from so-and-so, who bought it from you," and admitted that it was [the claimant's], he can no longer claim, "[So-and-so] bought it from you in my presence," or "[So-and-so] lived in it for one day in my presence," by virtue of a *migo* that had he wished he could have said at the outset, "It was never yours"; for we do not say a *migo* retroactively, as is evident later (Bava Batra 41b) in the case of the one who lived in the upper chamber in Kashta for four years, and said, "I bought it from so-and-so, who bought it from you." He came before Rabbi Chiyya, who said to him: "Bring witnesses that he lived in it even one day, and I will establish it in your possession." This implies that if he has no witnesses, he is not believed to say, "In my presence he lived in it one day," by virtue of a *migo* that had he wished he could have said, "I bought it from you"; since he already admitted that [the seller] did not buy it from [the claimant], he no longer has a *migo*, and we should not believe him regarding what he says now, on the grounds that he could have lied at the outset before he admitted — because [at that time] it did not occur to him that he would need this claim. And as for what Rav says there, "And I saw his reasoning, [that] my beloved, if he had said to him, 'In my presence he bought it from you,' he would have been believed, by virtue of a *migo* that had he wished he could have said, 'I bought it from you'" — he does not mean that he is still believed with this claim, but rather: if he had claimed so at the outset, before he admitted. And the same applies [vehe-hen, written "וה"ה"] — if he had claimed at the outset, "In my presence he lived in it for one day," that he would have been believed. And there is further proof from the end of [the chapter] Zeh Borer (Sanhedrin 31a), regarding that woman from whose hand a document emerged. She said, "I know about this document that it was paid, etc.," and Rav Nachman did not believe her. Rava said to him, "But if she had wished, she could have burned it!" [The answer is:] Since it has become established in court, we do not say "if she had wished, she could have burned it." Evidently, even though before we saw it in her hand she would have been believed to say that it was paid, by virtue of [the *migo* that] if she had wished she could have burned it, now that it has become established in court — meaning that we saw it in her hand — she is not believed, for there is no longer a *migo* here, since she now necessarily needs this claim that she is making, if she wants to exempt the borrower. And in the Commentary [of Rashi] there he explained: "it has become established" — that the document was validated. But this does not seem right to Ri, for what good does that do? For in any event, she could have burned it. And there is further proof, for we learned in the chapter Shevuat HaDayanin (Shevuot 38b): "[If one says,] 'I have a *maneh* in your possession,' and he said to him, 'Yes,' [and] the next day [the claimant] said to him, 'Give it to me,' [and he replied,] 'I already gave it to you' — he is exempt." And [the Gemara] challenges from it (there, 41a): According to the one who says that one who lends to his fellow with witnesses must repay him with witnesses — but here, since he demanded it in front of witnesses, it is as if he had lent it with witnesses, and yet it teaches that he is exempt! And what is the difficulty? Here it is different, for he is exempt by virtue of a *migo*: had he wished he could have said, "Yesterday there were never any such dealings." Rather, certainly in a case like this we do not say a *migo*. And as for what the Commentary [of Rashi] explained in the last chapter of Ketubot (109b, and there) regarding one who designated [a field] as a marker for another — that if he claimed and said, "I returned and bought it from him after I designated it as a marker in his name," he is believed, since "the mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted"; for since there are witnesses that it was his and it was seized from him, he has no claim except through the word of this one who designated it as a marker for him, and now he has gone back and said, "I bought it from you" — it does not seem right to Ri that in such a case we do not say a *migo*, as I explained, since because of what he could have claimed at first, he is not believed now. Rather, it seems to Ri that there too, he returned and held it for the years of *chazakah* after he designated it as a marker. And if you say: If he held it for the years of *chazakah*, it is obvious! What is Rabbi Yochanan teaching us, that he is believed? It is a Mishnah: "A *chazakah* that has a claim with it is a [valid] *chazakah*"! One may answer that one might have thought that he is not believed, since [the other] contested it with him before he held it for the years of *chazakah*, saying that it is his — [and one might have thought that] a person would not buy it after that. Therefore, [Rabbi Yochanan] teaches us [otherwise]. And likewise, that incident which [the Gemara] brings afterward is speaking of one who held it for the years of *chazakah*. And in our case, if the possessor had brought witnesses that [the seller] lived in it for one day, it seems to Rashba that the land should be established in his possession, even though there is no *migo*; in any case, we make a claim on behalf of the buyer, since the seller would have been believed to say, "I sold it to you," by virtue of a *migo* that had he wished he could have said, "It was never yours." And even though this buyer knew that it was [the claimant's] and he is like one witness, nevertheless it is a *migo*, as is implied later (Bava Batra 33b) regarding the ingot of Rabbi Abba: if he had not been obligated to take an oath and unable to swear, he would have been believed to say, "I seized what is mine," by virtue of a *migo* that had he wished he could have said, "I did not seize [anything]," and he would have been contradicting the witness; and here he is not obligated to take an oath, since one does not swear regarding land. And we find something like this at the end of [the chapter] HaMocher (later, Bava Batra 70a) regarding one who deposits with his fellow with a document — that although we do not make the claim "[the items] were lost through circumstances beyond his control" on behalf of the orphans, nevertheless we do make the claim "I returned it to you" on their behalf, since their father would have been believed with this claim, by virtue of a *migo* that had he wished he could have said, "They were lost through circumstances beyond my control." And Ri said that this is not similar to the case of HaMocher et HaBayit; for here, if the seller had wanted to prevail with this claim that "it was never yours," the buyer would not have prevented him, since he knew that it was [the claimant's]. Rabbeinu Chananel wrote: We have seen [that] our teachers the Geonim, of blessed memory, [held] that this possessor does not need to go down to litigation with the owner of the land; rather, the one who sold it to him goes down with him. But this does not seem right to Rashba, for any right that comes into his hand, the first sold to the second, and he cannot dismiss him and say to him, "You are not my litigant." And later we find explicitly, regarding the one who lived in the upper chamber in Kashta, that [the claimant] could not say to him, "You are not my litigant"; rather, had he found witnesses that that man lived in it for one day, Rabbi Chiyya would have established it in his possession:
